<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|trilobite|6480|Trimera}}</noinclude>{{smaller|sembling the thoracic segments, and with an axial raised portion, but united together. Of the under surface of a trilobite almost nothing was known until recently, and much still remains to be accurately determined. A well-developed lip-plate or hypostome had been recognized, but nothing further was known until 1870, when the under side of a species of ''Asaphus'', showing indistinct appendages, was described by Billings. Other investigators have pursued this subject, by means of sections of fossils, with the result of showing the presence of articulated appendages, or legs, and of other organs regarded as gills. The embryology of trilobites, so far as known, agrees most nearly with what has been accurately determined in the case of the horseshoe-crab. What may be inferred of the mode of life of trilobites is that probably their habits were like those of these crabs.—'''Dudley trilobite''', a common name of the trilobite ''Calymene blumenbachi'': so called from its abundance in the vicinity of Dudley, England.}}

'''trilobitic''' (trī-lọ̄-bit′ik), ''a.'' [< ''trilobite'' + ''-ic''.] Of or pertaining to trilobites; having the character of trilobites or affinity with them; containing trilobites, as geological strata.

'''trilocular''' (trī-lok′ụ̄-lạ̈r), ''a.'' [< L. ''tres'' (''tri-''), three, + ''loculus'', cell, + ''-ar''<sup>3</sup>.] Having three cells or compartments. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') In ''bot.'', having three cells or loculi: noting a pericarp. (''b'') In ''anat.'' and ''zoöl.'', having three loculi, compartments, or chamberlets: as, the ''trilocular'' heart of a reptile. Also ''triloculate''.}}

'''triloculate''' (trī-lok′ụ̄-lāt), ''a.'' [< L. ''tres'' (''tri-''), three, + ''loculus'', cell, + ''-ate''<sup>1</sup>.] Same as ''trilocular''.

'''trilogy''' (tril′ọ̄-ji), ''n.'' [= F. ''trilogie'', < Gr. τριλογία, a series of three tragedies, < τρεῖς (τρι-), three, + λόγος, a tale, story, narrative, speech, < λέγειν, say, tell: see ''logos'', and cf. ''-ology''.] Originally, in the Greek drama, a series of three

{{smaller block|Young Adam Cupid, he that shot so ''trim''
When King Cophetua loved the beggar-maid!
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., ii. 1. 13.}}}}

'''trim''' (trim), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''trimmed'', ppr. ''trimming''. [Early mod. E. also ''trimme'', ''trymme''; < ME. ''trimen'', ''trymen'', ''trumen'', < AS. ''trymian'', ''trymman'', make firm, strengthen, also set in order, array, prepare, < ''trum'', firm, strong: see ''trim'', ''a''.] I. ''trans.'' 1. To set in order; put in order; adjust; regulate; dispose.

{{smaller block|Beyng ryght wery of that Jorney, ffor the bestys that we rode vpon [were] ryght weke and ryght simple, and evyll ''trymed'' to Jorney with.
{{right|''Torkington'', Diarie of Eng. Travell, p. 55.}}}}

{{smaller block|Andrea Bragadino . . . had charge on that part of the castle, . . . ''trimming'' and digging out new flanckers for the better defence of the Arsenall.
{{right|''Hakluyt's Voyages'', II. i. 122.}}}}

{{smaller block|Back to my lonely home retire,
And light my lamp, and ''trim'' my fire.
{{right|''Scott'', Marmion, ii., Int.}}}}

{{smaller block|You don't care to be better than a bird ''trimming'' its feathers, and pecking about after what pleases it.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Felix Holt, x.}}}}

2. ''Naut.'', to adjust or balance, as a ship or boat, by distributing the weight of the lading so equally that it shall sit well on the water. {{smaller|A vessel is said to be ''trimmed'' by the head or by the stern respectively when the weight is so disposed as to make it draw more water toward the head than toward the stern, or the reverse.}}

{{smaller block|With all hands she did lighten her sterne, and ''trimme'' her head.
{{right|''Hakluyt's Voyages'', I. 448.}}}}

{{smaller block|My old friend . . . seated himself, and ''trimmed'' the boat with his coachman, who, being a very sober man, always}} tragedies, each forming a complete part or stage in a historical or poetical narrative; hence, any literary, dramatic, or operatic work consisting of a sequence of three parts, each complete and independent save in its relation to the general theme. {{smaller|Thus, the name ''trilogy'' is given to Shakspere's "Henry VI.," and to Schiller's "Wallenstein."}}

'''Trilophodon''' (trī-lof′ọ̄-don), ''n.'' [NL. (Falconer), < Gr. τρεῖς (τρι-), three, + λόφος, ridge, crest, + ὀδούς (ὀδοντ-) = E. ''tooth''.] A genus of mastodons whose molar teeth have crests in three rows. See ''Mastodontinæ''.

'''trilophodont''' (trī-lof′ọ̄-dont), ''a.'' [< NL. ''Trilophodon(t-)''.] Having three crests, as the teeth of certain mastodons; belonging or related to the genus ''Trilophodon''.

'''trilost''' (trī′lost), ''n.'' [Corn. ''trilost'', < ''tri'' (= W. ''tri''), three, + ''lost'' (= W. ''llost''), tail.] A term occurring only in the name ''cardinal trilost'', used locally in Cornwall for a sting-ray (''Trygon pastinaca'') having two spines on the tail.

'''triluminar†''' (trī-lū′mi-när), ''a.'' [< L. ''tres'' (''tri-''), three, + ''lumen'' (''-in-''), light, + ''-ar''<sup>3</sup>. Cf. ML. ''triluminare'', a candlestick with three branches.] Having three lights. ''Bailey'', 1727.

'''triluminous†''' (trī-lū′mi-nus), ''a.'' [< L. ''tres'' (''tri-''), three, + ''lumen'' (''-in-''), light, + ''-ous''.] Same as ''triluminar''. ''Bailey'', 1727.

{{smaller block|serves for ballast on these occasions.
{{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 383.}}}}

{{smaller block|''Trim'' the Boat and sit quiet, stern Charon reply'd.
{{right|''Prior'', Bibo and Charon.}}}}

3. To fit out; equip; furnish, especially with clothes; hence, to dress; deck: sometimes with ''up'' or ''forth''.

{{smaller block|The Harte, vice admiralle, with the Paunce and Sir Andrewe Dudley, being but single manned, had a greate conflicte with three Scottishe shippes, beeyng double manned and ''trimmed'' with ordinaunce. ''Fabyan'', Chron., an. 1546.}}

{{smaller block|''Trimm'd'' like a younker prancing to his love.
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen VI., ii. 1. 24.}}}}

{{smaller block|See, the jolly clerk
Appears, ''trimm'd'' like a ruffian.
{{right|''Ford'', Perkin Warbeck, iii. 4.}}}}

4. Specifically, to embellish with ornaments; decorate, as with ribbons, fringe, etc.

{{smaller block|Who reades Plutarchs eyther historie or philosophy, shall finde hee ''trymmeth'' both theyr garments with gards of Poesie. ''Sir P. Sidney'', Apol. for Poetrie, p. 59.}}

{{smaller block|The Lady Mayoress was dressed in green velvet, lined with white satin, ''trimmed'' with gold fringe and a border of Brussels lace. ''First Year of a Silken Reign'', p. 69.}}

5. To reduce to a neat or orderly state, as by clipping, paring, pruning, lopping, or otherwise removing superfluous or disfiguring parts.

{{smaller block|I ''trymme'', as a man dothe his heare or his busshe. . . . ''Trymme'' my busshe, barber, for I intende to go amongest ladyes to day. ''Palsgrave'', p. 762.}}

'''trim''' (trim), ''a.'' [Early mod. E. also ''trimme'', ''trym'', ''trymme''; an altered form, after the verb, of *''trum'', < ME. ''trum'' (only in comp. ''mistrum'', ''untrum''), < AS. ''trum'', firm, strong, = OLG. ''trim'', in the deriv. ''betrimmed'', ''betrimmd'', decked, trimmed, adorned, ''trimmke'', an affected, overdressed person; root unknown.] '''1'''†. Firm; strong.

{{smaller block|It taketh no rote in a briery place, ne in marice, nether in the sande that fleeteth awaye, but it requireth a pure, a ''trymme'', and a substaunciall grounde.
{{right|''J. Udall'', On Jas. i.}}}}

'''2.''' In good order or condition; properly disposed, equipped, or qualified; good; excellent; fine: often used ironically.

{{smaller block|Thirteene ''trim'' barkes throughlie furnished and appointed with good mariners and men of warre.
{{right|''Holinshed'', Chron., Edw. III., an. 1372.}}
I, be Gis, twold be ''trim'' wether,
And if it were not for this mist.
{{right|''Mariage of Witt and Wisdome.'' (''Nares'', under ''gis.'')}}
A ''trim'' exploit, a manly enterprise,
To conjure tears up in a poor maid's eyes
With your derision! ''Shak.'', M. N. D., iii. 2. 157.
The Dr. gave us a sermon this morning, in an elegant and ''trim'' discourse on the 39th Psalm.
{{right|''Evelyn'', To Dr. Bentley.}}}}

'''3.''' Neat; spruce; smart.

{{smaller block|I will make thee ''trim''
With flowers and garlands that were meant for him.
{{right|''Fletcher'', Faithful Shepherdess, iii. 1.}}
He put his hand around her waste
Soe small, so tight, and ''trim''.
{{right|''Robin Hood and the Tanner's Daughter'' (Child's Ballads, V. 335).}}
But there were ''trim'', cheerful villages, too, with a neat}}

{{smaller block|Before I went to bed, the barber come to ''trim'' me and wash me, and so to bed, in order to my being clean to-morrow.
{{right|''Pepys'', Diary, I. 187.}}
She inquired when the gardener was to come and ''trim'' the borders.
{{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Shirley, vii.}}}}

'''6.''' To cut off in the process of bookbinding: said of the ragged edges of paper or the bolts of book-sections.—'''7.''' To remove by clipping, pruning, or paring; lop or cut: with ''off'' or ''away'': as, to ''trim off'' shoots from a hedge.—'''8.''' In ''carp.'', to dress, as timber; make smooth; fit.—'''9.''' To rebuke; reprove sharply; also, to beat; thrash: sometimes indelicately applied to a woman. Compare ''untrimmed'', 2. [Colloq.]

{{smaller block|An she would be cool'd, sir, let the soldiers ''trim'' her.
{{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''), False One, ii. 3.}}
Soh! Sir Anthony ''trims'' my master: he is afraid to reply to his father—then vents his spleen on poor Fag.
{{right|''Sheridan'', The Rivals, ii. 1.}}}}

'''10.''' To spend or waste in trimming: with ''away''. See II.

{{smaller block|He who would hear what ev'ry fool cou'd say,
Would never fix his thought, but ''trim'' his time ''away''.
{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}

{{smaller|'''Rough-trimmed''', having only the protruding parts of leaves cut off, but not cut smooth: said of the edges of books.—'''To trim the shore''', to follow the shore closely: said of a school of fish.—'''To trim the yards''' or '''sails''', to brace the yards so that the wind will strike the sails at the suitable angle.—'''To trim up''', to put in order; arrange; garnish, as a costume or any part of it.—'''Trimmed edges''', the edges of books whose leaves are cut off smoothly. ='''Syn.''' '''1.''' To arrange.—'''3''' and '''4.''' To adorn, garnish, array, trick out.}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To keep an even balance: hold {{smaller block|or handsome parsonage and gray church set in the midst.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Felix Holt, Int.}}}}

'''trim''' (trim), ''adv.'' [Early mod. E. also ''trimme;'' < ''trim, a.''] In a trim manner; trimly.

a middle course or position, especially in a contest between parties, so as to seem to incline to neither, or to both alike: from the nautical meaning. See I., 2.

{{smaller block|He commends Atticus for his ''Trimming'', and Tully for his Cowardise, and speaks meanly of the Bravery of Cato.
{{right|''Jeremy Collier'', Short View (ed. 1698), p. 195.}}}}

{{smaller block|He ''trimmed'', as he said, as the temperate zone ''trims'' between intolerable heat and intolerable cold—as a good government ''trims'' between despotism and anarchy—as a pure church ''trims'' between the errors of the Papists and those of the Anabaptists.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Sir W. Temple.}}}}

'''To trim sharp''' (''naut.''), to haul up to the wind, and brace the yards sharp.

{{smaller block|The next Morning we again ''trimm'd sharp'', and made the best of our way to the Lobos de la Mar.
{{right|''Dampier'', Voyages, I. 145.}}}}

'''trim''' (trim), ''n.'' [< ''trim'', ''v.''] 1. Adjustment; order; condition; arrangement.

{{smaller block|And tooke them in the ''trim''
Of an encounter.
{{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, v. 565.}}}}

{{smaller block|Ere dusk fires were lit up stairs and below, the kitchen was in perfect ''trim''; Hannah and I were dressed, and all was in readiness.
{{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Jane Eyre, xxxiv.}}}}

2. ''Naut.'', the state of a ship, or of her cargo, ballast, spars, etc., with reference to her fitness for sailing.

{{smaller block|A nobler ship did never swim,
And you shall see her in full ''trim'':
I'll set, my friends, to do you honor,
Set every inch of sail upon her.
{{right|''Wordsworth'', The Wagoner, ii.}}}}

{{smaller block|We . . . prepared to get everything in ''trim'' for a long stay.
{{right|''R. H. Dana, Jr.'', Before the Mast, p. 301.}}}}

{{smaller block|When they had trimmed, but not yet with the capstan, Arents called to the captain, who returned an answer implying that the ship had come up again, and that the ''trim'' as it was would serve.
{{right|''W. C. Russell'', Death Ship, xxiii.}}}}

3. Mode of appearance or equipment; guise; garb; especially, the becoming or prescribed mode of dress, ornament, etc.; the fashion; full dress; of a ship, full sail.

{{smaller block|I'd court Bellona in her horrid ''trim'',
As if she were a mistress.
{{right|''Massinger'', Bondman, i. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|Uncomb'd his locks, and squalid his attire,
Unlike the ''trim'' of love and gay desire.
{{right|''Dryden'', Pal. and Arc., i. 540.}}}}

{{smaller block|"First we must put you in ''trim''." "In ''trim!''" said Morton, "what do you mean?" "Why, we must put on these rough bracelets [handcuffs]." ''Scott'', Old Mortality, xii.}}

4†. Dress; trapping; ornament.

{{smaller block|Death himself in all his horrid ''trims''.
{{right|''Fletcher'', Bonduca, iv. 3.}}}}

{{smaller block|Virtue, though in rags, may challenge more
Than vice set off with all the ''trim'' of greatness.
{{right|''Massinger'', Bondman, v. 3.}}}}

5. Nature; character; sort; stamp.

{{smaller block|And they
Did all that men of their own ''trim''
Are wont to do to please their whim.
{{right|''Shelley'', Peter Bell the Third, iv.}}}}

{{smaller block|"Why, kings are kittle cattle to shoe behind, as we say in the north," replied the Duke; "but his wife knows his ''trim'', and I have not the least doubt that the matter is quite certain." ''Scott'', Heart of Mid-Lothian, xxxviii.}}

6. In ''carp.'', the visible woodwork or finish of a house, as the base-boards, door- and window-casings, etc.

{{smaller block|No wood having been used in construction except for floors, doors, and ''trim''.
{{right|''New York Evening Post'', April 14, 1884.}} '''Out of trim''', not in good order; not evenly balanced: specifically said of a vessel with reference to uneven stowage of her cargo.—'''Trim of the masts''' (''naut.''), the position of the masts in regard to the ship and to one another, as near or distant, far forward or aft, upright or raking.}}

¶
'''trimacular''' (trī-mak′ū-lär), ''a.'' [< L. ''tres'' (''tri-''), three, + ''macula'', spot, + ''-ar''<sup>3</sup>.] Same as ''trimaculated''. ''Encyc. Dict.''

'''trimaculated''' (trī-mak′ū-lā-ted), ''a.'' [< L. ''tres'' (''tri-''), three, + ''macula'', spot, + ''-ate''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>. Cf. ''trammel''.] Marked with three spots.

{{smaller block|''Trimaculated'' Wrasse; . . . On each side of the lower part of the back fin were two large spots, and between the fin and the tail another.
{{right|''Pennant'', Brit. Zoöl. (ed. 1776), III. 248.}}}}

'''trimastigate''' (trī-mas′ti-gāt), ''a.'' [< Gr. τρεῖς (τρι-), three, + μάστιξ (μαστιγ-), whip, scourge, + ''-ate''<sup>1</sup>.] Having three flagella, as an infusorian; triflagellate.

'''trimembral''' (trī-mem′brạl), ''a.'' [< LL. ''trimembris'' (> Sp. It. ''trimembre''), having three sets of limbs, triple-membered, < L. ''tres'' (''tri-''), three, + ''membrum'', member: see ''member''.] Having or consisting of three members.

'''trimenstre†''', ''a.'' [ME. ''trymenstre'' for *''trimestre'', < L. ''trimestris'', of three months: see ''trimester''.] Trimestrial; specifically, ripening three months after sowing.

{{smaller block|''Trymenstre'' seede in erthe is nowe to strie. {{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 61.}}}}

'''trimensual''' (trī-men′s̮ū-a̤l), ''a.'' [< L. ''tres'' (''tri-''), three, + ''mensis'', month: see ''mensual''.] Happening every three months.

'''Trimera''' (trim′ẹ-rä̤), ''n. pl.'' [NL., neut. pl. of *''trimerus'': see ''trimerous''.] In ''entom.'': (''a'') A<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
